The Ayeyarwady bulbul (Pycnonotus blanfordi) begins life as an altricial nestling emerging from an incubated egg that weighs approximately 3.44 grams [Ww0 = approximately 3.44 grams] at hatching. This initial wet weight is derived from egg dimensions typical of the closely related Pycnonotus finlaysoni, whose eggs measure 20.3 to 22.1 millimeters in length and 14.6 to 15.2 millimeters in width. The developing embryo undergoes organogenesis within the calcareous shell and relies entirely on its yolk reserves until it hatches. Field observations indicate that the incubation period and the precise age at hatching are temperature-dependent; when eggs are incubated at a consistent temperature of 39 °C [T = 39 °C], the nestlings emerge after 11.5 days [ab = 11.5 days]. This relatively short embryonic development is typical of many small-bodied passerines within the Pycnonotidae family and underscores the rapid transition from an albumen-buffered embryo to a parental-fed chick. The newly hatched nestling is entirely dependent on both parents for brooding and provisioning, with its body mass increasing rapidly during the first week of life as it transitions from yolk absorption to first exogenous feeding.

Under the prevailing thermal conditions of the dry forests of central Myanmar, where ambient temperatures frequently reach 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C], the developmental schedule of nestling Ayeyarwady bulbuls is notably compressed. Sexual maturation in this species begins relatively early compared to other Southeast Asian passerines; captive-reared individuals have been documented reaching puberty at approximately 30 days after hatching [tp = approximately 30 days after hatching] at a temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]. This rapid gonadal maturation is accompanied by the completion of feather development and the attainment of near-adult body mass. In contrast, reproductive maturity in the sense of first breeding is deferred considerably: the time since birth at first brood is approximately 401.5 days [tR = approximately 401.5 days], a delay that reflects the extended period required for territory acquisition, pair bonding, and the accumulation of sufficient body condition to support egg production and subsequent parental care. at a temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]This pattern, in which puberty precedes first reproduction by over a year, is consistent with a life-history strategy that prioritizes somatic growth and social maturation before initiating the energetically demanding process of reproduction.

Adult body mass in the Ayeyarwady bulbul exhibits pronounced sexual dimorphism, with females reaching a maximum recorded adult weight of 33.3 grams [Wwi = 33.3 grams] and males attaining a significantly heavier ultimate wet weight of 36.8 grams [Wwi = 36.8 grams]. This difference in mass, amounting to approximately 10 percent of male body weight, is likely driven by the energetic demands of reproduction; females allocate substantial resources to egg formation and incubation, while males may invest more heavily in territorial defense and courtship displays. The species' basal metabolic requirements have been measured under controlled laboratory conditions: when maintained at a thermoneutral temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C], the maximum basal metabolic rate recorded is 55.29 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 55.29 milliliters of oxygen per hour]. This relatively modest oxygen consumption is consistent with the mass-specific metabolic rates of other small passerines in the Pycnonotidae family and likely reflects an adaptation to the warm, humid environments these birds typically inhabit, where thermoregulatory costs are comparatively low.

The reproductive strategy of Pycnonotus blanfordi is characterized by a moderate output of eggs across multiple nesting attempts within a single breeding season. At a stable ambient temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C], females typically lay between 2 and 3 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = between 2 and 3 eggs per clutch] and, under favorable conditions, they produce approximately 2 clutches annually [F_R_i = approximately 2 clutches annually]. This reproductive rate, which combines modest clutch sizes with multiple broods, allows the species to offset relatively high nest predation rates common in its lowland forest and scrubland habitats. After a successful hatching event, the nestlings grow rapidly and undergo a critical developmental milestone well before they achieve independence. Fledging, defined as the point at which the developing chick leaves the nest and achieves its first sustained flight, occurs at approximately 10 days after hatching [tx = approximately 10 days after hatching] when maintained at this same temperature at a temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]. This early fledging age is notably short for a passerine of this body size and may represent an adaptation to reduce the window of vulnerability to predators within the nest.

Longevity data for the Ayeyarwady bulbul, derived from both wild and captive populations, indicate that these birds are relatively short-lived compared to many temperate-zone passerines. At a constant temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C], the oldest documented individuals have been recorded reaching a maximum lifespan of approximately ten years [am = approximately ten years], though most wild birds likely survive for considerably less time due to predation, disease, and food scarcity. This lifespan is consistent with published values for other members of the genus Pycnonotus and reflects a fast-paced life history characterized by early maturation, high reproductive effort, and relatively early senescence. Following successful fledging, the parental provisioning period ends gradually as the young develop flight skills and foraging competence, eventually achieving nutritional independence. The species' life cycle thus progresses from the zygote stage through incubation, a brief nestling phase, fledgling independence, and juvenile dispersal, culminating in the attainment of sexual maturity and entry into the breeding population, with natural mortality typically occurring after multiple breeding seasons.
